title: Complaint: Roman doctors are not consistent when answering Protestant charges
source_text: LI. Sed quod maxime querimur illud est, Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores in hac quaestione non satis sibi ipsis constare. Nam quum Protestantium argumentis, aut accusationibus, ipsis occurrendum est, testantur se non negare fidelibus & justis omnem de gratia Dei certitudinem: se quidem hic non agnoscere certitudinem illam quae fidei divinae dicitur, sed tamen admittere certitudinem aliam inferioris generis, nempe, moralem, juxta quosdam, quae in perfectioribus formidinem excludat: aut saltem, juxta plures, conjecturalem, quae semper cum aliqua formidine juncta sit, nisi adsit specialis quaedam revelatio: Et istam tamen tantam, ut non sinat hominem haesitare atque fluctuare, nec illum ancipitem & suspensum relinquat, & sic abunde sufficiat ad conscientiae pacem gignendam & fovendam, & hominem spirituali laetitia mulcendum. Adeoque palam affirmant fideles, pios & justos non debere de sua justitia, & remissione peccatorum suorum ambiguos & dubios haerere, verum certam de illa concipere fiduciam, quam si nondum adepti sint, eorum officium est ad eam precibus & votis frequentibus, & studio bonorum operum contendere.
pass_a_gloss: But what we most complain of is this, that the doctors of the Roman Church are not sufficiently consistent with themselves in this question. For when they must meet Protestant arguments or accusations, they testify that they do not deny to the faithful and just every certainty concerning God’s grace: that they indeed do not here acknowledge that certainty which is called of divine faith, but nevertheless admit another certainty of an inferior kind—namely moral, according to some, which in the more perfect excludes fear; or at least, according to many, conjectural, which is always joined with some fear unless a certain special revelation is present: and yet so great that it does not allow a person to hesitate and fluctuate, nor leave him doubtful and suspended, and so abundantly suffices for generating and fostering peace of conscience and soothing the person with spiritual joy. And so they openly affirm that the faithful, pious, and just ought not to remain ambiguous and doubtful concerning their righteousness and the remission of their sins, but to conceive a certain trust concerning it, which if they have not yet attained, it is their duty to contend toward it by frequent prayers and vows and by the pursuit of good works.
pass_b_english: Under Protestant fire Rome grants peace-giving moral or conjectural certainty and a duty to pursue it.
Le Blanc’s complaint is inconsistency with how they speak when on the attack.
